title: Handling Stream Cancellation
text: Both endpoints MUST maintain flow control state for the stream in the unterminated direction until that direction enters a terminal state.

title: Stream Final Size
text: The receiver MUST use the final size of the stream to account for all bytes sent on the stream in its connection-level flow controller.

title: Stream Final Size
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send data on a stream at or beyond the final size.

title: Stream Final Size
text: If a RESET_STREAM or STREAM frame is received indicating a change in the final size for the stream, an endpoint SHOULD respond with an error of type FINAL_SIZE_ERROR; see Section 11 for details on error handling.

title: Stream Final Size
text: A receiver SHOULD treat receipt of data at or beyond the final size as an error of type FINAL_SIZE_ERROR, even after a stream is closed.

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: If either is received, the connection MUST be closed immediately with a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR if the offending value was received in a transport parameter or of type FRAME_ENCODING_ERROR if it was received in a frame; see Section 10.2.

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: Endpoints MUST NOT exceed the limit set by their peer.

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: An endpoint that receives a frame with a stream ID exceeding the limit it has sent MUST treat this as a connection error of type STREAM_LIMIT_ERROR; see Section 11 for details on error handling.

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: MAX_STREAMS frames that do not increase the stream limit MUST be ignored.

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: An endpoint that is unable to open a new stream due to the peer's limits SHOULD send a STREAMS_BLOCKED frame (Section 19.14).

title: Controlling Concurrency
text: An endpoint MUST NOT wait to receive this signal before advertising additional credit, since doing so will mean that the peer will be blocked for at least an entire round trip, and potentially indefinitely if the peer chooses not to send STREAMS_BLOCKED frames.

title: Connection ID
text: Connection IDs MUST NOT contain any information that can be used by an external observer (that is, one that does not cooperate with the issuer) to correlate them with other connection IDs for the same connection.

title: Connection ID
text: As a trivial example, this means the same connection ID MUST NOT be issued more than once on the same connection.

title: Connection ID
text: An endpoint MUST NOT use the same IP address and port for multiple concurrent connections with zero-length connection IDs, unless it is certain that those protocol features are not in use.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: The sequence number on each newly issued connection ID MUST increase by 1.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: When an endpoint issues a connection ID, it MUST accept packets that carry this connection ID for the duration of the connection or until its peer invalidates the connection ID via a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame (Section 19.16).

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint SHOULD ensure that its peer has a sufficient number of available and unused connection IDs.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MUST NOT provide more connection IDs than the peer's limit.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MAY send connection IDs that temporarily exceed a peer's limit if the NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame also requires the retirement of any excess, by including a sufficiently large value in the Retire Prior To field.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: After processing a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame and adding and retiring active connection IDs, if the number of active connection IDs exceeds the value advertised in its active_connection_id_limit transport parameter, an endpoint MUST close the connection with an error of type CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint SHOULD supply a new connection ID when the peer retires a connection ID.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: If an endpoint provided fewer connection IDs than the peer's active_connection_id_limit, it MAY supply a new connection ID when it receives a packet with a previously unused connection ID.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MAY limit the total number of connection IDs issued for each connection to avoid the risk of running out of connection IDs; see Section 10.3.2.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MAY also limit the issuance of connection IDs to reduce the amount of per-path state it maintains, such as path validation status, as its peer might interact with it over as many paths as there are issued connection IDs.

title: Issuing Connection IDs
text: An endpoint that initiates migration and requires non-zero-length connection IDs SHOULD ensure that the pool of connection IDs available to its peer allows the peer to use a new connection ID on migration, as the peer will be unable to respond if the pool is exhausted.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: Endpoints SHOULD retire connection IDs when they are no longer actively using either the local or destination address for which the connection ID was used.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: The endpoint SHOULD continue to accept the previously issued connection IDs until they are retired by the peer.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: If the endpoint can no longer process the indicated connection IDs, it MAY close the connection.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: Upon receipt of an increased Retire Prior To field, the peer MUST stop using the corresponding connection IDs and retire them with RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames before adding the newly provided connection ID to the set of active connection IDs.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: An endpoint SHOULD limit the number of connection IDs it has retired locally for which RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames have not yet been acknowledged.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: An endpoint SHOULD allow for sending and tracking a number of RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames of at least twice the value of the active_connection_id_limit transport parameter.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MUST NOT forget a connection ID without retiring it, though it MAY choose to treat having connection IDs in need of retirement that exceed this limit as a connection error of type CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MUST NOT forget a connection ID without retiring it, though it MAY choose to treat having connection IDs in need of retirement that exceed this limit as a connection error of type CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR.

title: Consuming and Retiring Connection IDs
text: Endpoints SHOULD NOT issue updates of the Retire Prior To field before receiving RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames that retire all connection IDs indicated by the previous Retire Prior To value.

title: Matching Packets to Connections
text: Invalid packets that lack strong integrity protection, such as Initial, Retry, or Version Negotiation, MAY be discarded.

title: Matching Packets to Connections
text: An endpoint MUST generate a connection error if processing the contents of these packets prior to discovering an error, or fully revert any changes made during that processing.

title: Client Packet Handling
text: The client MAY drop these packets, or it MAY buffer them in anticipation of later packets that allow it to compute the key.

title: Client Packet Handling
text: The client MAY drop these packets, or it MAY buffer them in anticipation of later packets that allow it to compute the key.

title: Client Packet Handling
text: If a client receives a packet that uses a different version than it initially selected, it MUST discard that packet.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: If a server receives a packet that indicates an unsupported version and if the packet is large enough to initiate a new connection for any supported version, the server SHOULD send a Version Negotiation packet as described in Section 6.1.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: A server MAY limit the number of packets to which it responds with a Version Negotiation packet.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: Servers MUST drop smaller packets that specify unsupported versions.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: Servers SHOULD respond with a Version Negotiation packet, provided that the datagram is sufficiently long.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: If a server refuses to accept a new connection, it SHOULD send an Initial packet containing a CONNECTION_CLOSE frame with error code CONNECTION_REFUSED.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: If the packet is a 0-RTT packet, the server MAY buffer a limited number of these packets in anticipation of a late-arriving Initial packet.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: Clients are not able to send Handshake packets prior to receiving a server response, so servers SHOULD ignore any such packets.

title: Server Packet Handling
text: Servers MUST drop incoming packets under all other circumstances.

title: Considerations for Simple Load Balancers
text: A server in a deployment that does not implement a solution to maintain connection continuity when the client address changes SHOULD indicate that migration is not supported by using the disable_active_migration transport parameter.

title: Considerations for Simple Load Balancers
text: Server deployments that use this simple form of load balancing MUST avoid the creation of a stateless reset oracle; see Section 21.11.

title: Version Negotiation
text: Clients that support multiple QUIC versions SHOULD ensure that the first UDP datagram they send is sized to the largest of the minimum datagram sizes from all versions they support, using PADDING frames (Section 19.1) as necessary.

title: Sending Version Negotiation Packets
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send a Version Negotiation packet in response to receiving a Version Negotiation packet.

title: Sending Version Negotiation Packets
text: A server MAY limit the number of Version Negotiation packets it sends.

title: Handling Version Negotiation Packets
text: A client that supports only this version of QUIC MUST abandon the current connection attempt if it receives a Version Negotiation packet, with the following two exceptions.

title: Handling Version Negotiation Packets
text: A client MUST discard any Version Negotiation packet if it has received and successfully processed any other packet, including an earlier Version Negotiation packet.

title: Handling Version Negotiation Packets
text: A client MUST discard a Version Negotiation packet that lists the QUIC version selected by the client.

title: Using Reserved Versions
text: Endpoints MAY add reserved versions to any field where unknown or unsupported versions are ignored to test that a peer correctly ignores the value.

title: Using Reserved Versions
text: Endpoints MAY send packets with a reserved version to test that a peer correctly discards the packet.

title: Cryptographic and Transport Handshake
text: The cryptographic handshake MUST provide the following properties:

title: Cryptographic and Transport Handshake
text: Endpoints MUST explicitly negotiate an application protocol.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: This Destination Connection ID MUST be at least 8 bytes in length.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: Until a packet is received from the server, the client MUST use the same Destination Connection ID value on all packets in this connection.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: Once a client has received a valid Initial packet from the server, it MUST discard any subsequent packet it receives on that connection with a different Source Connection ID.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: A client MUST change the Destination Connection ID it uses for sending packets in response to only the first received Initial or Retry packet.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: A server MUST set the Destination Connection ID it uses for sending packets based on the first received Initial packet.

title: Negotiating Connection IDs
text: Any further changes to the Destination Connection ID are only permitted if the values are taken from NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames; if subsequent Initial packets include a different Source Connection ID, they MUST be discarded.

title: Authenticating Connection IDs
text: The values provided by a peer for these transport parameters MUST match the values that an endpoint used in the Destination and Source Connection ID fields of Initial packets that it sent (and received, for servers).

title: Authenticating Connection IDs
text: Endpoints MUST validate that received transport parameters match received connection ID values.

title: Authenticating Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MUST treat the absence of the initial_source_connection_id transport parameter from either endpoint or the absence of the original_destination_connection_id transport parameter from the server as a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR.

title: Authenticating Connection IDs
text: An endpoint MUST treat the following as a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR or PROTOCOL_VIOLATION:

title: Transport Parameters
text: An endpoint MUST treat receipt of a transport parameter with an invalid value as a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR.

title: Transport Parameters
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send a parameter more than once in a given transport parameters extension.

title: Transport Parameters
text: An endpoint SHOULD treat receipt of duplicate transport parameters as a connection error of type TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: The definition of a new transport parameter (Section 7.4.2) MUST specify whether storing the transport parameter for 0-RTT is mandatory, optional, or prohibited.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: A client MUST NOT use remembered values for the following parameters: ack_delay_exponent, max_ack_delay, initial_source_connection_id, original_destination_connection_id, preferred_address, retry_source_connection_id, and stateless_reset_token.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: The client MUST use the server's new values in the handshake instead; if the server does not provide new values, the default values are used.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: A client that attempts to send 0-RTT data MUST remember all other transport parameters used by the server that it is able to process.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: If 0-RTT data is accepted by the server, the server MUST NOT reduce any limits or alter any values that might be violated by the client with its 0-RTT data.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: In particular, a server that accepts 0-RTT data MUST NOT set values for the following parameters (Section 18.2) that are smaller than the remembered values of the parameters.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: The applicable subset of transport parameters that permit the sending of application data SHOULD be set to non-zero values for 0-RTT.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: A server MAY store and recover the previously sent values of the max_idle_timeout, max_udp_payload_size, and disable_active_migration parameters and reject 0-RTT if it selects smaller values.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: A server MUST reject 0-RTT data if the restored values for transport parameters cannot be supported.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: When sending frames in 0-RTT packets, a client MUST only use remembered transport parameters; importantly, it MUST NOT use updated values that it learns from the server's updated transport parameters or from frames received in 1-RTT packets.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: When sending frames in 0-RTT packets, a client MUST only use remembered transport parameters; importantly, it MUST NOT use updated values that it learns from the server's updated transport parameters or from frames received in 1-RTT packets.

title: Values of Transport Parameters for 0-RTT
text: A server MAY treat the use of updated transport parameters in 0-RTT as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

title: New Transport Parameters
text: An endpoint MUST ignore transport parameters that it does not support.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: Implementations MUST support buffering at least 4096 bytes of data received in out-of-order CRYPTO frames.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: Endpoints MAY choose to allow more data to be buffered during the handshake.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: If an endpoint does not expand its buffer, it MUST close the connection with a CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED error code.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: Once the handshake completes, if an endpoint is unable to buffer all data in a CRYPTO frame, it MAY discard that CRYPTO frame and all CRYPTO frames received in the future, or it MAY close the connection with a CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED error code.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: Once the handshake completes, if an endpoint is unable to buffer all data in a CRYPTO frame, it MAY discard that CRYPTO frame and all CRYPTO frames received in the future, or it MAY close the connection with a CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED error code.

title: Cryptographic Message Buffering
text: Packets containing discarded CRYPTO frames MUST be acknowledged because the packet has been received and processed by the transport even though the CRYPTO frame was discarded.

title: Address Validation
text: Therefore, after receiving packets from an address that is not yet validated, an endpoint MUST limit the amount of data it sends to the unvalidated address to three times the amount of data received from that address.

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: Additionally, an endpoint MAY consider the peer address validated if the peer uses a connection ID chosen by the endpoint and the connection ID contains at least 64 bits of entropy.

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: Prior to validating the client address, servers MUST NOT send more than three times as many bytes as the number of bytes they have received.

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: For the purposes of avoiding amplification prior to address validation, servers MUST count all of the payload bytes received in datagrams that are uniquely attributed to a single connection.

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: Clients MUST ensure that UDP datagrams containing Initial packets have UDP payloads of at least 1200 bytes, adding PADDING frames as necessary.

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: To prevent this deadlock, clients MUST send a packet on a Probe Timeout (PTO); see Section 6.2 of [QUIC-RECOVERY].

title: Address Validation during Connection Establishment
text: Specifically, the client MUST send an Initial packet in a UDP datagram that contains at least 1200 bytes if it does not have Handshake keys, and otherwise send a Handshake packet.

title: Token Construction
text: A token sent in a NEW_TOKEN frame or a Retry packet MUST be constructed in a way that allows the server to identify how it was provided to a client.

title: Address Validation Using Retry Packets
text: This token MUST be repeated by the client in all Initial packets it sends for that connection after it receives the Retry packet.

title: Address Validation Using Retry Packets
text: Instead, the server SHOULD immediately close (Section 10.2) the connection with an INVALID_TOKEN error.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A server MAY provide clients with an address validation token during one connection that can be used on a subsequent connection.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: The client MUST include the token in all Initial packets it sends, unless a Retry replaces the token with a newer one.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: The client MUST NOT use the token provided in a Retry for future connections.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: Servers MAY discard any Initial packet that does not carry the expected token.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: Thus, a token SHOULD have an expiration time, which could be either an explicit expiration time or an issued timestamp that can be used to dynamically calculate the expiration time.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A token issued with NEW_TOKEN MUST NOT include information that would allow values to be linked by an observer to the connection on which it was issued.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A server MUST ensure that every NEW_TOKEN frame it sends is unique across all clients, with the exception of those sent to repair losses of previously sent NEW_TOKEN frames.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: Information that allows the server to distinguish between tokens from Retry and NEW_TOKEN MAY be accessible to entities other than the server.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: When connecting to a server for which the client retains an applicable and unused token, it SHOULD include that token in the Token field of its Initial packet.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A client MUST NOT include a token that is not applicable to the server that it is connecting to, unless the client has the knowledge that the server that issued the token and the server the client is connecting to are jointly managing the tokens.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A client MAY use a token from any previous connection to that server.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: In comparison, a token obtained in a Retry packet MUST be used immediately during the connection attempt and cannot be used in subsequent connection attempts.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: A client SHOULD NOT reuse a token from a NEW_TOKEN frame for different connection attempts.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: When a server receives an Initial packet with an address validation token, it MUST attempt to validate the token, unless it has already completed address validation.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: If the token is invalid, then the server SHOULD proceed as if the client did not have a validated address, including potentially sending a Retry packet.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: If the validation succeeds, the server SHOULD then allow the handshake to proceed.

title: Address Validation for Future Connections
text: Clients MAY use tokens obtained on one connection for any connection attempt using the same version.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: An address validation token MUST be difficult to guess.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: For this design to work, the token MUST be covered by integrity protection against modification or falsification by clients.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: Tokens sent in Retry packets SHOULD include information that allows the server to verify that the source IP address and port in client packets remain constant.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: Tokens sent in NEW_TOKEN frames MUST include information that allows the server to verify that the client IP address has not changed from when the token was issued.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: If the client IP address has changed, the server MUST adhere to the anti-amplification limit; see Section 8.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: To protect against such attacks, servers MUST ensure that replay of tokens is prevented or limited.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: Servers SHOULD ensure that tokens sent in Retry packets are only accepted for a short time, as they are returned immediately by clients.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: Tokens that are provided in NEW_TOKEN frames (Section 19.7) need to be valid for longer but SHOULD NOT be accepted multiple times.

title: Address Validation Token Integrity
text: Servers are encouraged to allow tokens to be used only once, if possible; tokens MAY include additional information about clients to further narrow applicability or reuse.

title: Path Validation
text: An endpoint MAY include other frames with the PATH_CHALLENGE and PATH_RESPONSE frames used for path validation.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: An endpoint MAY send multiple PATH_CHALLENGE frames to guard against packet loss.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: However, an endpoint SHOULD NOT send multiple PATH_CHALLENGE frames in a single packet.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: An endpoint SHOULD NOT probe a new path with packets containing a PATH_CHALLENGE frame more frequently than it would send an Initial packet.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: The endpoint MUST use unpredictable data in every PATH_CHALLENGE frame so that it can associate the peer's response with the corresponding PATH_CHALLENGE.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: An endpoint MUST expand datagrams that contain a PATH_CHALLENGE frame to at least the smallest allowed maximum datagram size of 1200 bytes, unless the anti-amplification limit for the path does not permit sending a datagram of this size.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: To ensure that the path MTU is large enough, the endpoint MUST perform a second path validation by sending a PATH_CHALLENGE frame in a datagram of at least 1200 bytes.

title: Initiating Path Validation
text: Unlike other cases where datagrams are expanded, endpoints MUST NOT discard datagrams that appear to be too small when they contain PATH_CHALLENGE or PATH_RESPONSE.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: On receiving a PATH_CHALLENGE frame, an endpoint MUST respond by echoing the data contained in the PATH_CHALLENGE frame in a PATH_RESPONSE frame.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: An endpoint MUST NOT delay transmission of a packet containing a PATH_RESPONSE frame unless constrained by congestion control.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: A PATH_RESPONSE frame MUST be sent on the network path where the PATH_CHALLENGE frame was received.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: This requirement MUST NOT be enforced by the endpoint that initiates path validation, as that would enable an attack on migration; see Section 9.3.3.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: An endpoint MUST expand datagrams that contain a PATH_RESPONSE frame to at least the smallest allowed maximum datagram size of 1200 bytes.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: However, an endpoint MUST NOT expand the datagram containing the PATH_RESPONSE if the resulting data exceeds the anti-amplification limit.

title: Path Validation Responses
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send more than one PATH_RESPONSE frame in response to one PATH_CHALLENGE frame; see Section 13.3.

title: Successful Path Validation
text: However, the endpoint MUST initiate another path validation with an expanded datagram to verify that the path supports the required MTU.

title: Failed Path Validation
text: Endpoints SHOULD abandon path validation based on a timer.

title: Failed Path Validation
text: A value of three times the larger of the current PTO or the PTO for the new path (using kInitialRtt, as defined in [QUIC-RECOVERY]) is RECOMMENDED.

title: Failed Path Validation
text: An endpoint that has no valid network path to its peer MAY signal this using the NO_VIABLE_PATH connection error, noting that this is only possible if the network path exists but does not support the required MTU (Section 14).

title: Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MUST NOT initiate connection migration before the handshake is confirmed, as defined in Section 4.1.2 of [QUIC-TLS].

title: Connection Migration
text: If the peer sent the disable_active_migration transport parameter, an endpoint also MUST NOT send packets (including probing packets; see Section 9.1) from a different local address to the address the peer used during the handshake, unless the endpoint has acted on a preferred_address transport parameter from the peer.

title: Connection Migration
text: If the peer violates this requirement, the endpoint MUST either drop the incoming packets on that path without generating a Stateless Reset or proceed with path validation and allow the peer to migrate.

title: Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MUST perform path validation (Section 8.2) if it detects any change to a peer's address, unless it has previously validated that address.

title: Connection Migration
text: When an endpoint has no validated path on which to send packets, it MAY discard connection state.

title: Connection Migration
text: An endpoint capable of connection migration MAY wait for a new path to become available before discarding connection state.

title: Connection Migration
text: If a client receives packets from an unknown server address, the client MUST discard these packets.

title: Probing a New Path
text: An endpoint MAY probe for peer reachability from a new local address using path validation (Section 8.2) prior to migrating the connection to the new local address.

title: Initiating Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MAY defer path validation until after a peer sends the next non-probing frame to its new address.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: If the recipient permits the migration, it MUST send subsequent packets to the new peer address and MUST initiate path validation (Section 8.2) to verify the peer's ownership of the address if validation is not already underway.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: If the recipient permits the migration, it MUST send subsequent packets to the new peer address and MUST initiate path validation (Section 8.2) to verify the peer's ownership of the address if validation is not already underway.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MAY send data to an unvalidated peer address, but it MUST protect against potential attacks as described in Sections 9.3.1 and 9.3.2.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MAY send data to an unvalidated peer address, but it MUST protect against potential attacks as described in Sections 9.3.1 and 9.3.2.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MAY skip validation of a peer address if that address has been seen recently.

title: Responding to Connection Migration
text: After verifying a new client address, the server SHOULD send new address validation tokens (Section 8) to the client.

title: On-Path Address Spoofing
text: To protect the connection from failing due to such a spurious migration, an endpoint MUST revert to using the last validated peer address when validation of a new peer address fails.

title: On-Path Address Spoofing
text: If an endpoint has no state about the last validated peer address, it MUST close the connection silently by discarding all connection state.

title: On-Path Address Spoofing
text: For instance, an endpoint MAY send a Stateless Reset in response to any further incoming packets.

title: Off-Path Packet Forwarding
text: In response to an apparent migration, endpoints MUST validate the previously active path using a PATH_CHALLENGE frame.

title: Off-Path Packet Forwarding
text: An endpoint that receives a PATH_CHALLENGE on an active path SHOULD send a non-probing packet in response.

title: Loss Detection and Congestion Control
text: Packets sent on the old path MUST NOT contribute to congestion control or RTT estimation for the new path.

title: Loss Detection and Congestion Control
text: On confirming a peer's ownership of its new address, an endpoint MUST immediately reset the congestion controller and round-trip time estimator for the new path to initial values (see Appendices A.3 and B.3 of [QUIC-RECOVERY]) unless the only change in the peer's address is its port number.

title: Loss Detection and Congestion Control
text: Because port-only changes are commonly the result of NAT rebinding or other middlebox activity, the endpoint MAY instead retain its congestion control state and round-trip estimate in those cases instead of reverting to initial values.

title: Loss Detection and Congestion Control
text: This timer SHOULD be set as described in Section 6.2.1 of [QUIC-RECOVERY] and MUST NOT be more aggressive.

title: Loss Detection and Congestion Control
text: This timer SHOULD be set as described in Section 6.2.1 of [QUIC-RECOVERY] and MUST NOT be more aggressive.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: At any time, endpoints MAY change the Destination Connection ID they transmit with to a value that has not been used on another path.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: An endpoint MUST NOT reuse a connection ID when sending from more than one local address -- for example, when initiating connection migration as described in Section 9.2 or when probing a new network path as described in Section 9.1.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: Similarly, an endpoint MUST NOT reuse a connection ID when sending to more than one destination address.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: Due to network changes outside the control of its peer, an endpoint might receive packets from a new source address with the same Destination Connection ID field value, in which case it MAY continue to use the current connection ID with the new remote address while still sending from the same local address.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: An endpoint SHOULD NOT initiate migration with a peer that has requested a zero-length connection ID, because traffic over the new path might be trivially linkable to traffic over the old one.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: Changing address can cause a peer to reset its congestion control state (see Section 9.4), so addresses SHOULD only be changed infrequently.

title: Privacy Implications of Connection Migration
text: To ensure that migration is possible and packets sent on different paths cannot be correlated, endpoints SHOULD provide new connection IDs before peers migrate; see Section 5.1.1.

title: Server's Preferred Address
text: If a client receives packets from a new server address when the client has not initiated a migration to that address, the client SHOULD discard these packets.

title: Communicating a Preferred Address
text: Servers MAY communicate a preferred address of each address family (IPv4 and IPv6) to allow clients to pick the one most suited to their network attachment.

title: Communicating a Preferred Address
text: Once the handshake is confirmed, the client SHOULD select one of the two addresses provided by the server and initiate path validation (see Section 8.2).

title: Communicating a Preferred Address
text: As soon as path validation succeeds, the client SHOULD begin sending all future packets to the new server address using the new connection ID and discontinue use of the old server address.

title: Communicating a Preferred Address
text: If path validation fails, the client MUST continue sending all future packets to the server's original IP address.

title: Migration to a Preferred Address
text: A client that migrates to a preferred address MUST validate the address it chooses before migrating; see Section 21.5.3.

title: Sending ACK Frames
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send a non-ack-eliciting packet in response to a non-ack-eliciting packet, even if there are packet gaps that precede the received packet.

title: Acknowledgment Frequency

title: Managing ACK Ranges
text: ACK frames SHOULD always acknowledge the most recently received packets, and the more out of order the packets are, the more important it is to send an updated ACK frame quickly, to prevent the peer from declaring a packet as lost and spuriously retransmitting the frames it contains.

text: Once an endpoint successfully receives a packet with a given packet number, it MUST discard all packets in the same packet number space with higher packet numbers if they cannot be successfully unprotected with either the same key, or -- if there is a key update -- a subsequent packet protection key; see Section 6.

title: Receiving Protected Packets
text: Similarly, a packet that appears to trigger a key update but cannot be unprotected successfully MUST be discarded.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A client therefore MUST NOT use 0-RTT for application data unless specifically requested by the application that is in use.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: An application protocol that uses QUIC MUST include a profile that defines acceptable use of 0-RTT; otherwise, 0-RTT can only be used to carry QUIC frames that do not carry application data.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A client MAY wish to apply additional restrictions on what data it sends prior to the completion of the TLS handshake.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A client SHOULD stop sending 0-RTT data if it receives an indication that 0-RTT data has been rejected.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A server MUST NOT use 0-RTT keys to protect packets; it uses 1-RTT keys to protect acknowledgments of 0-RTT packets.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A client MUST NOT attempt to decrypt 0-RTT packets it receives and instead MUST discard them.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: A client MUST NOT attempt to decrypt 0-RTT packets it receives and instead MUST discard them.

title: Use of 0-RTT Keys
text: Once a client has installed 1-RTT keys, it MUST NOT send any more 0-RTT packets.

title: Receiving Out-of-Order Protected Packets
text: Endpoints in either role MUST NOT decrypt 1-RTT packets from their peer prior to completing the handshake.

title: Receiving Out-of-Order Protected Packets
text: A server MUST NOT process incoming 1-RTT protected packets before the TLS handshake is complete.

title: Receiving Out-of-Order Protected Packets
text: Received packets protected with 1-RTT keys MAY be stored and later decrypted and used once the handshake is complete.

title: Receiving Out-of-Order Protected Packets
text: The server MAY retain these packets for later decryption in anticipation of receiving a ClientHello.

title: Receiving Out-of-Order Protected Packets
text: Even if it has 1-RTT secrets, a client MUST NOT process incoming 1-RTT protected packets before the TLS handshake is complete.

title: Key Update
text: Once the handshake is confirmed (see Section 4.1.2), an endpoint MAY initiate a key update.

title: Key Update
text: Endpoints MUST NOT send a TLS KeyUpdate message.

title: Key Update
text: Endpoints MUST treat the receipt of a TLS KeyUpdate message as a connection error of type 0x010a, equivalent to a fatal TLS alert of unexpected_message; see Section 4.8.

title: Initiating a Key Update
text: An endpoint MUST NOT initiate a key update prior to having confirmed the handshake (Section 4.1.2).

title: Initiating a Key Update
text: An endpoint MUST NOT initiate a subsequent key update unless it has received an acknowledgment for a packet that was sent protected with keys from the current key phase.

title: Initiating a Key Update
text: An endpoint MUST retain old keys until it has successfully unprotected a packet sent using the new keys.

title: Initiating a Key Update
text: An endpoint SHOULD retain old keys for some time after unprotecting a packet sent using the new keys.

title: Responding to a Key Update
text: The endpoint MUST update its send keys to the corresponding key phase in response, as described in Section 6.1.

title: Responding to a Key Update
text: Sending keys MUST be updated before sending an acknowledgment for the packet that was received with updated keys.

title: Responding to a Key Update
text: An endpoint MAY treat such consecutive key updates as a connection error of type KEY_UPDATE_ERROR.

title: Responding to a Key Update
text: An endpoint that receives an acknowledgment that is carried in a packet protected with old keys where any acknowledged packet was protected with newer keys MAY treat that as a connection error of type KEY_UPDATE_ERROR.

title: Timing of Receive Key Generation
text: Endpoints responding to an apparent key update MUST NOT generate a timing side-channel signal that might indicate that the Key Phase bit was invalid (see Section 9.5).

title: Timing of Receive Key Generation
text: An endpoint MAY generate new keys as part of packet processing, but this creates a timing signal that could be used by an attacker to learn when key updates happen and thus leak the value of the Key Phase bit.

title: Timing of Receive Key Generation
text: For a short period after a key update completes, up to the PTO, endpoints MAY defer generation of the next set of receive packet protection keys.

title: Timing of Receive Key Generation
text: Once generated, the next set of packet protection keys SHOULD be retained, even if the packet that was received was subsequently discarded.

title: Timing of Receive Key Generation
text: For this reason, endpoints MUST be able to retain two sets of packet protection keys for receiving packets: the current and the next.

title: Sending with Updated Keys
text: Packets with higher packet numbers MUST be protected with either the same or newer packet protection keys than packets with lower packet numbers.

title: Sending with Updated Keys
text: An endpoint that successfully removes protection with old keys when newer keys were used for packets with lower packet numbers MUST treat this as a connection error of type KEY_UPDATE_ERROR.

title: Receiving with Different Keys
text: An endpoint MAY allow a period of approximately the Probe Timeout (PTO; see [QUIC-RECOVERY]) after promoting the next set of receive keys to be current before it creates the subsequent set of packet protection keys.

title: Receiving with Different Keys
text: These updated keys MAY replace the previous keys at that time.

title: Receiving with Different Keys
text: Endpoints SHOULD wait three times the PTO before initiating a key update after receiving an acknowledgment that confirms that the previous key update was received.

title: Receiving with Different Keys
text: An endpoint SHOULD retain old read keys for no more than three times the PTO after having received a packet protected using the new keys.

title: Receiving with Different Keys
text: After this period, old read keys and their corresponding secrets SHOULD be discarded.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: Endpoints MUST count the number of encrypted packets for each set of keys.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: If the total number of encrypted packets with the same key exceeds the confidentiality limit for the selected AEAD, the endpoint MUST stop using those keys.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: Endpoints MUST initiate a key update before sending more protected packets than the confidentiality limit for the selected AEAD permits.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: If a key update is not possible or integrity limits are reached, the endpoint MUST stop using the connection and only send stateless resets in response to receiving packets.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: It is RECOMMENDED that endpoints immediately close the connection with a connection error of type AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED before reaching a state where key updates are not possible.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: In addition to counting packets sent, endpoints MUST count the number of received packets that fail authentication during the lifetime of a connection.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: If the total number of received packets that fail authentication within the connection, across all keys, exceeds the integrity limit for the selected AEAD, the endpoint MUST immediately close the connection with a connection error of type AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED and not process any more packets.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: Endpoints that limit the size of packets MAY use higher confidentiality and integrity limits; see Appendix B for details.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: Future analyses and specifications MAY relax confidentiality or integrity limits for an AEAD.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: Any TLS cipher suite that is specified for use with QUIC MUST define limits on the use of the associated AEAD function that preserves margins for confidentiality and integrity.

title: Limits on AEAD Usage
text: That is, limits MUST be specified for the number of packets that can be authenticated and for the number of packets that can fail authentication.

title: Security of Initial Messages
text: Implementations SHOULD use caution in relying on any data that is contained in Initial packets that is not otherwise authenticated.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: Unless another mechanism is used for agreeing on an application protocol, endpoints MUST use ALPN for this purpose.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: When using ALPN, endpoints MUST immediately close a connection (see Section 10.2 of [QUIC-TRANSPORT]) with a no_application_protocol TLS alert (QUIC error code 0x0178; see Section 4.8) if an application protocol is not negotiated.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: While [ALPN] only specifies that servers use this alert, QUIC clients MUST use error 0x0178 to terminate a connection when ALPN negotiation fails.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: An application protocol MAY restrict the QUIC versions that it can operate over.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: Servers MUST select an application protocol compatible with the QUIC version that the client has selected.

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: The server MUST treat the inability to select a compatible application protocol as a connection error of type 0x0178 (no_application_protocol).

title: Protocol Negotiation
text: Similarly, a client MUST treat the selection of an incompatible application protocol by a server as a connection error of type 0x0178.

title: QUIC Transport Parameters Extension
text: Endpoints MUST send the quic_transport_parameters extension; endpoints that receive ClientHello or EncryptedExtensions messages without the quic_transport_parameters extension MUST close the connection with an error of type 0x016d (equivalent to a fatal TLS missing_extension alert, see Section 4.8).

title: QUIC Transport Parameters Extension
text: Endpoints MUST send the quic_transport_parameters extension; endpoints that receive ClientHello or EncryptedExtensions messages without the quic_transport_parameters extension MUST close the connection with an error of type 0x016d (equivalent to a fatal TLS missing_extension alert, see Section 4.8).

title: QUIC Transport Parameters Extension
text: Endpoints MUST NOT send this extension in a TLS connection that does not use QUIC (such as the use of TLS with TCP defined in [TLS13]).

title: QUIC Transport Parameters Extension
text: A fatal unsupported_extension alert MUST be sent by an implementation that supports this extension if the extension is received when the transport is not QUIC.

title: Removing the EndOfEarlyData Message
text: Clients MUST NOT send the EndOfEarlyData message.

title: Removing the EndOfEarlyData Message
text: A server MUST treat receipt of a CRYPTO frame in a 0-RTT packet as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

title: Prohibit TLS Middlebox Compatibility Mode
text: A client MUST NOT request the use of the TLS 1.3 compatibility mode.

title: Prohibit TLS Middlebox Compatibility Mode
text: A server SHOULD treat the receipt of a TLS ClientHello with a non-empty legacy_session_id field as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_VIOLATION.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: Endpoints MUST implement and use the replay protections described in [TLS13], however it is recognized that these protections are imperfect.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: These MUST NOT be used to communicate application semantics between endpoints; clients MUST treat them as opaque values.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: These MUST NOT be used to communicate application semantics between endpoints; clients MUST treat them as opaque values.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: An application protocol that uses QUIC MUST describe how the protocol uses 0-RTT and the measures that are employed to protect against replay attack.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: QUIC extensions MUST either describe how replay attacks affect their operation or prohibit the use of the extension in 0-RTT.

title: Replay Attacks with 0-RTT
text: Application protocols MUST either prohibit the use of extensions that carry application semantics in 0-RTT or provide replay mitigation strategies.

title: Packet Reflection Attack Mitigation
text: First, the packet containing a ClientHello MUST be padded to a minimum size.

title: Header Protection Analysis
text: Future header protection variants based on this construction MUST use a PRF to ensure equivalent security guarantees.

title: Header Protection Timing Side Channels
text: For authentication to be free from side channels, the entire process of header protection removal, packet number recovery, and packet protection removal MUST be applied together without timing and other side channels.

title: Header Protection Timing Side Channels
text: For the sending of packets, construction and protection of packet payloads and packet numbers MUST be free from side channels that would reveal the packet number or its encoded size.

title: Header Protection Timing Side Channels
text: After receiving a key update, an endpoint SHOULD generate and save the next set of receive packet protection keys, as described in Section 6.3.

title: Key Diversity
text: To preserve this separation, a new version of QUIC SHOULD define new labels for key derivation for packet protection key and IV, plus the header protection keys.

title: Key Diversity
text: New QUIC versions SHOULD define a new salt value used in calculating initial secrets.

title: Generating RTT Samples
text: To avoid generating multiple RTT samples for a single packet, an ACK frame SHOULD NOT be used to update RTT estimates if it does not newly acknowledge the largest acknowledged packet.

title: Generating RTT Samples
text: An RTT sample MUST NOT be generated on receiving an ACK frame that does not newly acknowledge at least one ack-eliciting packet.

title: Estimating min_rtt
text: min_rtt MUST be set to the latest_rtt on the first RTT sample.

title: Estimating min_rtt
text: min_rtt MUST be set to the lesser of min_rtt and latest_rtt (Section 5.1) on all other samples.

title: Estimating min_rtt
text: Endpoints SHOULD set the min_rtt to the newest RTT sample after persistent congestion is established.

title: Estimating min_rtt
text: Endpoints MAY reestablish the min_rtt at other times in the connection, such as when traffic volume is low and an acknowledgment is received with a low acknowledgment delay.

title: Estimating min_rtt
text: Implementations SHOULD NOT refresh the min_rtt value too often since the actual minimum RTT of the path is not frequently observable.

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar
text: To account for this, the endpoint SHOULD ignore max_ack_delay until the handshake is confirmed, as defined in Section 4.1.2 of [QUIC-TLS].

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar
text: Therefore, prior to handshake confirmation, an endpoint MAY ignore RTT samples if adjusting the RTT sample for acknowledgment delay causes the sample to be less than the min_rtt.

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar
text: MAY ignore the acknowledgment delay for Initial packets, since these acknowledgments are not delayed by the peer (Section 13.2.1 of [QUIC-TRANSPORT]);

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar
text: SHOULD ignore the peer's max_ack_delay until the handshake is confirmed;

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar
text: MUST use the lesser of the acknowledgment delay and the peer's max_ack_delay after the handshake is confirmed; and

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar

title: Estimating smoothed_rtt and rttvar

title: Acknowledgment-Based Detection
text: Implementations with adaptive time thresholds MAY choose to start with smaller initial reordering thresholds to minimize recovery latency.

title: Packet Threshold
text: The RECOMMENDED initial value for the packet reordering threshold (kPacketThreshold) is 3, based on best practices for TCP loss detection [RFC5681] [RFC6675].

title: Packet Threshold
text: In order to remain similar to TCP, implementations SHOULD NOT use a packet threshold less than 3; see [RFC5681].

title: Time Threshold
text: Once a later packet within the same packet number space has been acknowledged, an endpoint SHOULD declare an earlier packet lost if it was sent a threshold amount of time in the past.

title: Time Threshold
text: To avoid declaring packets as lost too early, this time threshold MUST be set to at least the local timer granularity, as indicated by the kGranularity constant.

title: Time Threshold
text: If packets sent prior to the largest acknowledged packet cannot yet be declared lost, then a timer SHOULD be set for the remaining time.

title: Time Threshold
text: The RECOMMENDED time threshold (kTimeThreshold), expressed as an RTT multiplier, is 9/8.

title: Time Threshold
text: The RECOMMENDED value of the timer granularity (kGranularity) is 1 millisecond.

title: Time Threshold
text: Implementations MAY experiment with absolute thresholds, thresholds from previous connections, adaptive thresholds, or the including of RTT variation.

title: Probe Timeout
text: A PTO timer expiration event does not indicate packet loss and MUST NOT cause prior unacknowledged packets to be marked as lost.

title: Computing PTO
text: The PTO period MUST be at least kGranularity to avoid the timer expiring immediately.

title: Computing PTO
text: When ack-eliciting packets in multiple packet number spaces are in flight, the timer MUST be set to the earlier value of the Initial and Handshake packet number spaces.

title: Computing PTO
text: An endpoint MUST NOT set its PTO timer for the Application Data packet number space until the handshake is confirmed.

title: Computing PTO
text: A sender SHOULD restart its PTO timer every time an ack-eliciting packet is sent or acknowledged, or when Initial or Handshake keys are discarded (Section 4.9 of [QUIC-TLS]).

title: Computing PTO
text: When a PTO timer expires, the PTO backoff MUST be increased, resulting in the PTO period being set to twice its current value.

title: Computing PTO
text: The PTO timer MUST NOT be set if a timer is set for time threshold loss detection; see Section 6.1.2.

title: Handshakes and New Paths
text: Resumed connections over the same network MAY use the previous connection's final smoothed RTT value as the resumed connection's initial RTT.

title: Handshakes and New Paths
text: When no previous RTT is available, the initial RTT SHOULD be set to 333 milliseconds.

title: Handshakes and New Paths
text: A connection MAY use the delay between sending a PATH_CHALLENGE and receiving a PATH_RESPONSE to set the initial RTT (see kInitialRtt in Appendix A.2) for a new path, but the delay SHOULD NOT be considered an RTT sample.

title: Handshakes and New Paths
text: A connection MAY use the delay between sending a PATH_CHALLENGE and receiving a PATH_RESPONSE to set the initial RTT (see kInitialRtt in Appendix A.2) for a new path, but the delay SHOULD NOT be considered an RTT sample.

title: Handshakes and New Paths
text: When Initial or Handshake keys are discarded, the PTO and loss detection timers MUST be reset, because discarding keys indicates forward progress and the loss detection timer might have been set for a now-discarded packet number space.

title: Before Address Validation
text: If no additional data can be sent, the server's PTO timer MUST NOT be armed until datagrams have been received from the client because packets sent on PTO count against the anti-amplification limit.

title: Before Address Validation
text: That is, the client MUST set the PTO timer if the client has not received an acknowledgment for any of its Handshake packets and the handshake is not confirmed (see Section 4.1.2 of [QUIC-TLS]), even if there are no packets in flight.

title: Before Address Validation
text: When the PTO fires, the client MUST send a Handshake packet if it has Handshake keys, otherwise it MUST send an Initial packet in a UDP datagram with a payload of at least 1200 bytes.

title: Before Address Validation
text: When the PTO fires, the client MUST send a Handshake packet if it has Handshake keys, otherwise it MUST send an Initial packet in a UDP datagram with a payload of at least 1200 bytes.

title: Speeding up Handshake Completion
text: To speed up handshake completion under these conditions, an endpoint MAY, for a limited number of times per connection, send a packet containing unacknowledged CRYPTO data earlier than the PTO expiry, subject to the address validation limits in Section 8.1 of [QUIC-TRANSPORT].

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: When a PTO timer expires, a sender MUST send at least one ack-eliciting packet in the packet number space as a probe.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: An endpoint MAY send up to two full-sized datagrams containing ack-eliciting packets to avoid an expensive consecutive PTO expiration due to a single lost datagram or to transmit data from multiple packet number spaces.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: All probe packets sent on a PTO MUST be ack-eliciting.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: In addition to sending data in the packet number space for which the timer expired, the sender SHOULD send ack-eliciting packets from other packet number spaces with in-flight data, coalescing packets if possible.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: An endpoint SHOULD include new data in packets that are sent on PTO expiration.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: Previously sent data MAY be sent if no new data can be sent.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: Implementations MAY use alternative strategies for determining the content of probe packets, including sending new or retransmitted data based on the application's priorities.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: When there is no data to send, the sender SHOULD send a PING or other ack-eliciting frame in a single packet, rearming the PTO timer.

title: Sending Probe Packets
text: Alternatively, instead of sending an ack-eliciting packet, the sender MAY mark any packets still in flight as lost.

title: Handling Retry Packets
text: The client MAY compute an RTT estimate to the server as the time period from when the first Initial packet was sent to when a Retry or a Version Negotiation packet is received.

title: Handling Retry Packets

title: Congestion Control
text: If a sender uses a different controller than that specified in this document, the chosen controller MUST conform to the congestion control guidelines specified in Section 3.1 of [RFC8085].

title: Congestion Control
text: Unlike TCP, QUIC can detect the loss of these packets and MAY use that information to adjust the congestion controller or the rate of ACK-only packets being sent, but this document does not describe a mechanism for doing so.

title: Congestion Control
text: An endpoint MUST NOT send a packet if it would cause bytes_in_flight (see Appendix B.2) to be larger than the congestion window, unless the packet is sent on a PTO timer expiration (see Section 6.2) or when entering recovery (see Section 7.3.2).

title: Initial and Minimum Congestion Window
text: Endpoints SHOULD use an initial congestion window of ten times the maximum datagram size (max_datagram_size), while limiting the window to the larger of 14,720 bytes or twice the maximum datagram size.

title: Initial and Minimum Congestion Window
text: If the maximum datagram size changes during the connection, the initial congestion window SHOULD be recalculated with the new size.

title: Initial and Minimum Congestion Window
text: If the maximum datagram size is decreased in order to complete the handshake, the congestion window SHOULD be set to the new initial congestion window.

title: Initial and Minimum Congestion Window
text: The RECOMMENDED value is 2 * max_datagram_size.

title: Slow Start
text: The sender MUST exit slow start and enter a recovery period when a packet is lost or when the ECN-CE count reported by its peer increases.

title: Recovery
text: On entering a recovery period, a sender MUST set the slow start threshold to half the value of the congestion window when loss is detected.

title: Recovery
text: The congestion window MUST be set to the reduced value of the slow start threshold before exiting the recovery period.

title: Recovery
text: Implementations MAY reduce the congestion window immediately upon entering a recovery period or use other mechanisms, such as Proportional Rate Reduction [PRR], to reduce the congestion window more gradually.

title: Congestion Avoidance
text: A sender in congestion avoidance uses an Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD) approach that MUST limit the increase to the congestion window to at most one maximum datagram size for each congestion window that is acknowledged.

title: Ignoring Loss of Undecryptable Packets
text: Endpoints MAY ignore the loss of Handshake, 0-RTT, and 1-RTT packets that might have arrived before the peer had packet protection keys to process those packets.

title: Ignoring Loss of Undecryptable Packets
text: Endpoints MUST NOT ignore the loss of packets that were sent after the earliest acknowledged packet in a given packet number space.

title: Probe Timeout

title: Establishing Persistent Congestion

title: Establishing Persistent Congestion
text: Since network congestion is not affected by packet number spaces, persistent congestion SHOULD consider packets sent across packet number spaces.

title: Establishing Persistent Congestion
text: A sender that does not have state for all packet number spaces or an implementation that cannot compare send times across packet number spaces MAY use state for just the packet number space that was acknowledged.

title: Establishing Persistent Congestion
text: When persistent congestion is declared, the sender's congestion window MUST be reduced to the minimum congestion window (kMinimumWindow), similar to a TCP sender's response on an RTO [RFC5681].

title: Pacing

title: Pacing
text: To avoid delaying their delivery to the peer, packets containing only ACK frames SHOULD therefore not be paced.

text: When this occurs, the congestion window SHOULD NOT be increased in either slow start or congestion avoidance.

title: Discovering an HTTP/3 Endpoint

title: Connection Reuse

title: Extensions to HTTP/3

title: Extensions to HTTP/3

title: Intermediary-Encapsulation Attacks

title: Denial-of-Service Considerations

title: Denial-of-Service Considerations

title: Use of Compression

title: Use of Compression

title: Encoder
text: An encoder MAY insert any entry in the dynamic table it chooses; it is not limited to field lines it is compressing.

title: Encoder
text: An encoder MUST emit field representations in the order they appear in the input field section.

title: Limits on Dynamic Table Insertions
text: If the dynamic table does not contain enough room for a new entry without evicting other entries, and the entries that would be evicted are not evictable, the encoder MUST NOT insert that entry into the dynamic table (including duplicates of existing entries).

title: Blocked Streams
text: An encoder MUST limit the number of streams that could become blocked to the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS at all times.

title: Blocked Streams
text: If a decoder encounters more blocked streams than it promised to support, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

title: Avoiding Flow-Control Deadlocks
text: To avoid these deadlocks, an encoder SHOULD NOT write an instruction unless sufficient stream and connection flow-control credit is available for the entire instruction.

title: Decoder
text: The decoder MUST emit field lines in the order their representations appear in the encoded field section.

title: Blocked Decoding
text: While blocked, encoded field section data SHOULD remain in the blocked stream's flow-control window.

title: Blocked Decoding
text: If it encounters a Required Insert Count smaller than expected, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED; see Section 2.2.3.

title: Blocked Decoding
text: If it encounters a Required Insert Count larger than expected, it MAY treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

title: Completed Processing of a Field Section
text: After the decoder finishes decoding a field section encoded using representations containing dynamic table references, it MUST emit a Section Acknowledgment instruction (Section 4.4.1).

title: Abandonment of a Stream
text: A decoder with a maximum dynamic table capacity (Section 3.2.3) equal to zero MAY omit sending Stream Cancellations, because the encoder cannot have any dynamic table references.

title: Invalid References
text: If the decoder encounters a reference in a field line representation to a dynamic table entry that has already been evicted or that has an absolute index greater than or equal to the declared Required Insert Count (Section 4.5.1), it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

title: Invalid References
text: If the decoder encounters a reference in an encoder instruction to a dynamic table entry that has already been evicted, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Static Table
text: When the decoder encounters an invalid static table index in a field line representation, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

title: Static Table
text: If this index is received on the encoder stream, this MUST be treated as a connection error of type QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Dynamic Table
text: Therefore, duplicate entries MUST NOT be treated as an error by the decoder.

title: Dynamic Table Capacity and Eviction
text: The encoder MUST NOT cause a dynamic table entry to be evicted unless that entry is evictable; see Section 2.1.1.

title: Dynamic Table Capacity and Eviction
text: It is an error if the encoder attempts to add an entry that is larger than the dynamic table capacity; the decoder MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Maximum Dynamic Table Capacity
text: The encoder MUST NOT set a dynamic table capacity that exceeds this maximum, but it can choose to use a lower dynamic table capacity; see Section 4.3.1.

title: Maximum Dynamic Table Capacity

title: Maximum Dynamic Table Capacity

title: Maximum Dynamic Table Capacity

title: Maximum Dynamic Table Capacity

title: Prefixed Integers
text: QPACK implementations MUST be able to decode integers up to and including 62 bits long.

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: Each endpoint MUST initiate, at most, one encoder stream and, at most, one decoder stream.

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: Receipt of a second instance of either stream type MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR.

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: Closure of either unidirectional stream type MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: An endpoint MAY avoid creating an encoder stream if it will not be used (for example, if its encoder does not wish to use the dynamic table or if the maximum size of the dynamic table permitted by the peer is zero).

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: An endpoint MAY avoid creating a decoder stream if its decoder sets the maximum capacity of the dynamic table to zero.

title: Encoder and Decoder Streams
text: An endpoint MUST allow its peer to create an encoder stream and a decoder stream even if the connection's settings prevent their use.

title: Set Dynamic Table Capacity
text: The new capacity MUST be lower than or equal to the limit described in Section 3.2.3.

title: Set Dynamic Table Capacity
text: The decoder MUST treat a new dynamic table capacity value that exceeds this limit as a connection error of type QPACK_ENCODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Set Dynamic Table Capacity
text: This MUST NOT cause the eviction of entries that are not evictable; see Section 2.1.1.

title: Section Acknowledgment
text: If an encoder receives a Section Acknowledgment instruction referring to a stream on which every encoded field section with a non-zero Required Insert Count has already been acknowledged, this MUST be treated as a connection error of type QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Insert Count Increment
text: An encoder that receives an Increment field equal to zero, or one that increases the Known Received Count beyond what the encoder has sent, MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECODER_STREAM_ERROR.

title: Required Insert Count
text: If the decoder encounters a value of EncodedInsertCount that could not have been produced by a conformant encoder, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

title: Base
text: The value of Base MUST NOT be negative.

title: Base
text: An endpoint MUST treat a field block with a Sign bit of 1 as invalid if the value of Required Insert Count is less than or equal to the value of Delta Base.

title: Literal Field Line with Name Reference
text: When the 'N' bit is set, the encoded field line MUST always be encoded with a literal representation.

title: Literal Field Line with Name Reference
text: In particular, when a peer sends a field line that it received represented as a literal field line with the 'N' bit set, it MUST use a literal representation to forward this field line.

title: Never-Indexed Literals
text: An intermediary MUST NOT re-encode a value that uses a literal representation with the 'N' bit set with another representation that would index it.

title: Never-Indexed Literals
text: If QPACK is used for re-encoding, a literal representation with the 'N' bit set MUST be used.

title: Never-Indexed Literals
text: If HPACK is used for re-encoding, the never-indexed literal representation (see Section 6.2.3 of [RFC7541]) MUST be used.

title: Implementation Limits
text: These limits SHOULD be large enough to process the largest individual field the HTTP implementation can be configured to accept.

title: Implementation Limits
text: If an implementation encounters a value larger than it is able to decode, this MUST be treated as a stream error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED if on a request stream or a connection error of the appropriate type if on the encoder or decoder stream.
